paras: The lynching of Jack Roberts was the hanging in March 1881 of a man accused of shooting Thomas A. Greatorex at Durango, Colorado, carried out by what dispatches called a band of vigilantes. The first reports put the lynching at Durango on the night of March 25; a later St. Louis dispatch said vigilantes took him from two men who had captured him for a reward and hanged him to a tree. Newspapers across the country ran the story as a brief item, several describing Roberts as one of a band of "noted desperadoes"; none gave his race.

According to the Durango Record, reprinted in the Fremont County Record, the trouble began about 3 o'clock one morning, when two women quarreled in the Coliseum auditorium and Tom Lynch and Jack Roberts joined the affray. Greatorex, who had stayed behind after an entertainment, stepped in to help what he took to be a woman in distress and was struck on the head with a revolver by Roberts. The Record said Roberts then shot him in the back before he could rise and escaped through a side door. The "leading citizens of Durango" offered $500 for the capture of Roberts "dead or alive."

Greatorex died of the wound about ten days later; the Washington papers dated the shooting to the 6th and his death to the 16th. Those papers recalled him as a former Treasury messenger, the son of the artist Eliza Greatorex, who had made his home at Silverton.

A special to the Denver Times, telegraphed on March 26, reported that Roberts, "the murderer of Tom Greatorex, was lynched at Durango last night." The Sacramento Daily Record-Union put the lynching on Friday night, March 25. On April 2 the Fremont County Record said in its state news that Roberts had been "captured and lynched" the week before.

A fuller account came in a St. Louis dispatch of April 1 based on "advices from Durango." It said Thomas Nance and John Benning had captured Roberts a few days earlier and were taking him to Farmington when a band of vigilantes, "regulators" in one printing, overtook them. The vigilantes paid the two men the reward and hanged Roberts to a tree for the killing of Greatorex; none of the reports named them, gave their number or mentioned any officer.
No report of an inquest or of any arrest for the hanging appears in the coverage.

The Denver special ran within a day under "Lynched" in the Cheyenne Daily Leader and the Las Vegas Morning Gazette, and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer grouped it with a Walla Walla lynching under "High Life in the West." These items called Roberts only "the murderer" and gave no details.

In Washington the National Republican's "A Colorado Tragedy" and the Evening Star's "Killed in Colorado" told the story around Greatorex's career, adding that a telegram reported his killer caught and lynched. The New-York Tribune and the Portland Daily Press, drawing on an earlier letter from Durango, said instead that the killer, "a notorious gambler" in the Tribune's words, had escaped lynching by flight.

The St. Louis dispatch reached papers from Tucson to St. Paul and Washington by April 3 and weeklies in Montana, Kansas and Dakota by April 8. The dispatch called Roberts "that worthy" and one of a band of desperadoes who had long been a terror in southern Colorado. The Wheeling Register headlined it "A Noted Desperado Hanged by a Band of Vigilants," and the Arizona Weekly Citizen, which printed the name as "Jack Robertson," ran it as "Served Him Right."

Most printings of the Denver special put the lynching on the night of March 25, but the Las Vegas Morning Gazette's version said "night before last," and a Wheeling news note said Sunday. The first dispatches placed it at Durango, the St. Louis dispatch on the road toward Farmington.

Accounts of the shooting also differed: the local Record, written while Greatorex was alive, described a 3 a.m. affray in the Coliseum, the New York letter a street encounter at dusk on March 11. The Record credited the reward to citizens of Durango, the National Republican to citizens of Silverton.

Roberts was reported 'lynched' (A4, A7, A21) and, in the fuller St. Louis dispatch, taken from his captors by 'a band of vigilantes' or 'regulators' and hanged to a tree (A17, A30) for the killing of Greatorex; no number is given for the band, and nothing ties the killing to race.

A Denver Times special (A4, A5, A6), a separate St. Louis dispatch with 'advices from Durango' (A17, A30) and the Colorado state news of the Fremont County Record (A21) all report the lynching; two earlier New York items saying the killer escaped lynching by flight (A14, A15) rest on a letter written before his capture.

Washington and New York papers wrote about Greatorex ('A Colorado Tragedy,' 'Murder in Colorado'), mentioning the lynching only in passing or not at all.
The St. Louis wire called Roberts 'that worthy' and one of a band of 'noted desperadoes'; the Arizona Weekly Citizen headed it 'Served Him Right.'
